newsitem.title: UK: Mutant mouse offers answers about addiction, pain.
newsitem.headline: Mutant mouse offers answers about addiction, pain.

text.p: Genetically mutated mice that get no kick from morphine may offer a clue to heroin addiction, French scientists reported on Wednesday.

The mice get none of the pain-dulling benefits of morphine, but do not become addicted to it, either, Brigitte Kieffer of the Universite Louis Pasteur in Strasbourg and colleagues reported in the science journal Nature.
They were looking at three receptors in brain cells known to be affected by opioids -- chemicals such as morphine and heroin which are based on the drug opium.
Mice were bred that were normal except for a missing receptor, known as "mu".
They were given morphine and then subjected to painful tests. Others were given addictive doses of the drugs.
But they showed little response to the drug.
"Investigation of the behavioural effects of morphine reveals that a lack of mu receptors abolishes the analgesic effect of morphine," Kieffer's group wrote.
The other two receptors, known as delta and kappa, did not seem to be involved at all in reponses to the drugs.
Leslie Iversen, a pharmacologist at Oxford University, said the findings would help shed light on the addictive and pain-killing properties of opioids.
"The new findings are an important advance and provide yet another demonstration of the power of modern genetic engineering in attacking age-old biological problems," Iversen said.
